params.textField: The name of the disorders that involves an excess of endogenous (the body's own) or exogenous (administered) corticosteroids is *Cushing’s disease/syndrome* and results in the clinical picture that we examined in the last lesson, including mood face, protruding abdomen, thin extremities, muscle weakness from protein breakdown, and weight gain. But corticosteroid treatment can also cause *osteonecrosis* which is a death of a portion of a bone, and *yeast infections* due to the inhibition of the immune and inflammatory reactions as well as a list of side effects that would fill an entire page. The opposite condition can occur as well, after long term glucocorticoid treatment. An adrenal gland shortage of cortisol and other glucocorticoids is termed *Addison’s disease*, which involves depression, fatigue, anorexia (decreased ability to eat), and an inability to respond to stressful situations. This type of problem can occur if long term corticosteroid treatment is withdrawn too quickly. Remember that it is the glucocorticoids that work as a negative feedback, decreasing the hypothalamic release of *CRH* and the pituitary’s release of *ACTH*. It is often very difficult to convince these organs that we need to start the secretion again, so slow withdrawal of glucocorticoids like prednisone is absolutely essential. We can only live a few days without cortisol.

params.textField: You were just asked to remember two ‘corticosteroids’ (glucocorticoids) in this lesson, but what we know about those two drugs can be applied to most of the other corticosteroids. *prednisone* is a pro-drug that needs to be changed in the liver to the active form, *prednisolone*. Those are highly prescribed medications that reduce the immune and inflammatory response. If taken for long periods of time, those medications can cause the clinical picture known as *iatrogenic Cushing’s syndrome* and if they are withdrawn too quickly after long term use, they can cause the clinical picture similar to that of *Addison’s disease*. The other medication that is important to know from the stress axis is actually an antagonist of the mineralocorticoid, aldosterone, known as spironolactone, which we will cover in a later module.
